text:
A little over a year ago I decided to stick my toe in the HiRes Digital Audio pool. I didn’t have a boat load of Benjamin’s to sink into the endeavor but I did get the best my budget could afford. I got the HiBy R6 DAP and two IEM’s to go with it. The TinAudio T2’s and the BGVP DMG’S. Both are outstanding IEM’s but I had been hearing a lot of buzz about the hybrid electrostatic/DD Tin P1’s and was seriously considering going that way. The T2’s were a good buy and the P1’s were getting great reviews from uToobers I trust. Then about a month ago these BQEYZ Spring 1’s hit the market and the buzz shifted. I decided to give them a spin. If they weren’t a big enough improvement over the BGVP’s I could always return ‘em. Well they ain’t going anywhere. The advances in personal audio over the course of the last year have been remarkable. I’m not a big fan of Chinese stuff but they are getting a solid reputation for two of the markets I dabble in, HiRes Audio and folding knives. As for these Spring 1’s they f*ing rock. Amazing soundstage, crisp punchy bass, outstanding mids and perfectly fine highs (I say perfectly fine because I have tinnitus and my hearing craps out at about 15kHz). Every instrument has its place and is distinct. The first thing I listened to was Pink Floyd Meddle and it nearly brought tears to my eyes. For an investment of just under $200 (I got the 16 core silver cable upgrade, although the stock one is perfectly adequate) you really can’t go wrong. Can’t wait for next year.

I did have the opportunity to compare these with the Shuoer Tape hybrid IEM’s and it only took me about t minutes to box up the Tape’s and return them. The Tape’s were much brighter and lacking the warmth and soundstage of the Spring 1’s. Of course as with everything that is as subjective as audio YMMV.

text:
The Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure that I received works, but the tray design is really quite awful. I'm not going to return it, but the next time I buy a 3.5 inch HDD USB enclosure I will look elsewhere.

I own both the Thermaltake Max 5G (USB3) & Max 4 (USB2) HDD enclosures. I also have worked with one of the Sabrent "fan-ed" USB HDD enclosures. I cannot remember if it was USB 2 or 3.

The Sabrent enclosure was pretty good, other than the fact that the enclosure box "slid around" in its stand (the part that contacts the table/shelf).

The Thermaltake enclosures are the best and most everything about them is top notch. Unfortunately, Thermaltake no longer manufactures this sort of enclosure. They do still make BlacX USB docks. Those are docks, not enclosures.

Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure
------------------------------------------

First come the complaints.

Rosewill provided incorrect HDD screws/bolts. When working with PCs there are normally only 2 types of screws/bolts = coarse thread and fine thread. HDDs take coarse thread screws. The 4 screws the Rosewill provided looked like coarse thread screws, but they wouldn't go into my HDDs more then a couple of turns. I threw them out and used my own screws.

At this point I have tried 3 different 3.5 inch HDDs with the Rosewill RX304 enclosure and none of the HDDs were able to become fully seated within the HDD tray. By fully seated I mean that all 4 HDD screw holes line up with the screw holes of the HDD tray. I was never able to get more than 2 screws in. I used WD and Seagate HDDs.

But before trying to align the screw holes you have to get the HDD into the tray in the 1st place. THIS IS VERY DIFFICULT TO DO because the tray (at the top) is ever so slightly narrower then the HDD that is going into it. WhiskeyTangoFoxtrot??? I guess that I should try bending the tray wall outwards to make it permanently wider. As a buyer I'm supposed to doing this kind of BS maneuver? This is a very bad joke ... and it is on me. If I bend the tray wall outwards will I break something?

The mechanical engineer that designed this tray is going to hell when they die.

OK. So now the HDD is in the tray (with only 2 screws) and the SATA cables are attached. The SATA cable attachments are a whole other mediocre story, but they can be made to work, so we will continue.

One (or more) reviewer/s suggested that the air passage that remains after seating the HDD is not wide enough for decent air flow to the fan and then out of the case. I could be wrong, but I suspect that there is is just enough space for reasonable air flow.

Second comes the reasonably good part.

Once the HDD is in the tray and the tray (plus interface board) is reinserted into the enclosure box you can put the end on and attach it with 2 screws. This part of the procedure is OK, but nowhere near top quality. There is an internal rail inside the enclosure box that aligns the HDD/tray/interface board within said box. But, there are only 2 "keys" in the frame that go into the rail, so the HDD tray assembly is sorta slip/sliding around in the box until you get it fully inserted, at which time the end edge of the enclosure box mates up with an internal channel in the plastic front end.

So now we have the box fully assembled, and we put it in its stand (4 rubber "nubs" keep the box from slipping around, nice). We then cable up the enclosure's power and connect the USB 3 to a computer.

Once all of the above is done you get pretty good performance. On a 2 TB HDD I was able to read the outside tracks at 200 MB/sec. That's the same performance that I get with that HDD inside a computer cabled directly to the mobo. The USB 3 interface worked well for me.

On a slightly down note the program HDDScan could not read the SMART values through the interface board of the Rosewill RX304, but was able to read the SMART values through the interface board of a 2.5 inch Mediasonic USB 3 enclosure that I also own. Other programs may well be able to "penetrate" this USB interface to get SMART data ... who knows.

As I said at the start the Rosewill RX304 is OK, but I won't be buying any more of these units.
title: It works, but TERRIBLE tray design

text:
I have a steel roof home, which hinders the FM reception on my HD Radio receiver. Up until now I'd been piggy backing my reception off my flat Mohu TV window antenna with an amplifier. Note this window does not face the broadcast towers. But last week I realized my antenna had an FM trap, so I was excited try a switch to the Terk.

Unfortunately, the Terk doesn't perform as well as the Mohu, even using the amplifier and experimenting with different placements. However, I was motivated to revisit my old dipole wire antenna and use it with the amp. To my surprise, when experimenting with positioning, the dipole performed better than either of the newer antennas. I'd say about 1-2 bars better on my 5 bar meter, depending on which antenna I'm using, and the station.

I suppose the Terk would be okay if you have a good signal and want a modern looking antenna. However, for my needs, the dipole antenna does a better job.
title: Not as effective as standard dipole antenna

text:
When you order a $400 pair of headphones the last thing that you expect is for the manufacturer to take a bunch of shortcuts on quality, but this high-end pair of Technics headphones seem to be full of compromises and it almost seems like the company put more effort into marketing and packaging than it did in the final product.

The biggest letdown with this product is it's construction. It's almost entirely made of plastic, which is something that you might expect from a pair of $35 Bluetooth headphones, but not ones that sell for nearly $400. Obviously, the headphone is not going to be covered under warranty if the plastic construction breaks, and since it is mostly plastic, that is what is most likely to break first.

The other big compromises are the lack of the latest in Bluetooth technology, which is Bluetooth 5.0. There are plenty of headphones selling for far under $100 that use Bluetooth 5.0. Why not these? Charging is another issue. Rather than a fast charging USB-C connection or a convenient wireless charging connection there is a cheap and antiquated Micro-USB charger input. Again, fine for a cheap pair of headphones, but when you are talking about $400 headphones you expect MUCH better. The ear pads are also less comfortable than I would expect in this price class. They aren't horrible, but do not have the ultra soft, leather-like feel to them that you expect in high-end headphones.

On to the good things about these headphones... The packaging is really nice. If only the product was designed as well as the packing I would be so happy with this product. Bluetooth connectivity is flawless, but most $20 Bluetooth products can say the same. The ANC feature is both flexible and powerful. They do a great job at blocking out outside noise without affecting audio quality. From my limited experience with ANC headphones, these are the best I have tried thus far.

The audio quality is also quite impressive for a Bluetooth device. While it does not produce he best sound I have ever heard from a pair of corded headphones they are on par with the best Bluetooth headphones I have used. I would hesitate to say that they are THE best sounding Bluetooth headphones I have used though.

While these are "nice" Bluetooth headphones they come nowhere near what I would expect from something in this price class. They are about on par with what you would expect for a pair of Bluetooth headphones selling in the $180-$200 range, but that's it. The lack of latest features and the use of plastic throughout it's construction really rubs me the wrong way. If these sold at half of their current price I might give them a four star review. I think that I am being generous at giving them the three stars that they are getting though.
title: Mid-Range Quality At A High-End Price

text:
This outlet strip works o.k. Just don't take the description of the product too seriously. For one thing, it claims to provide a total of 2.4 Amps to each of it's 4 charging ports, but provides a total of only 4.2 Amps. Even a third grader can tell you that 2.4 x 4 is more than 4.2. So, the total amount of Amps per port is only about half of what is claimed. So, you can pretty much forget fast charging any of your devices if you have more than 3 items charging at the same time.

I'm not sure about the claim of the 2 AC outlets having "supper wide space". Maybe it means that you get more space while eating dinner? It also claims to feature "4 smart Micro USB ports". Nope. They are just regular sized USB ports, not micro, which would make no sense anyway.

Other than that, this "power strip", as they call it, is pretty unremarkable. It is missing a great number of functions that you would expect, even in it's price range. Some of the features that it does NOT include are: NO surge protection or line filtering, NO reset switch, NO on/off switch, No ability for the plug to swivel positions, NO LED to show if the charger outlets are working, NO clamps along the side of the unit to coil the cord around. NO warranty beyond 30 days and NO company contact information.

So, it's basically just a cheaply constructed Chinese product with only 2 AC outlets and maybe 2 outlets that will quick charge your phone at the same time. Nothing too exciting here.
title: Works O.K. Ignore Description Though

text:
Caveats: Routers are always hit or miss and if you read any review you will see (much like other products I guess) the 1 or 2 stars reviews complaining about having to reset the router, weak signal and so on. Every Netgear or TP-Link or Linksys routers I have had, they do great for a while and for some reason they just need an occasional and then a frequent reset till you decide it's time to upgrade. So, long term jury is out on this one much like other routers. Having used this in my house for under 24 hours, this router is performing as it should. I would recommend it based on my short experience. So, buy it with confidence. As for details, here's the approach I took.

I hooked up one unit as instructed and updated firmware and measured my up and down speed. I have a real basic internet speed so I know this unit is capable of doing more. I used the same speedtest off the web for all my tests for consistency. In general, I found this unit to be as fast as my old (read, real old) unit in the same room and the room next door. Two rooms down, this unit is not strong as a dedicated router and speeds began to drop. So, I added the second unit in the basement (I couldn't tell much difference between ethernet backhaul versus wifi but I think that has a lot to do with my basic internet package from my ISP. I anticipate better results when I upgrade). My third and final unit I felt wasn't even necessary. Even the basement unit provided sufficient coverage in my upstairs bedroom which never worked with my single router. I had three so I went ahead and put it in one of the bedrooms upstairs.

The app is good, you need a cloud id. YouTube does a good job of all functions so all good. Any questions, ask away. Overall, a great buy so far. Fingers crossed and I hope I don't have to come back and update my review (in a negative direction).
title: Cautiously optimistic

text:
These work great! My smart tv kept loosing connection to the wifi, so had to find a wired solution.

Living in an apartment I don't have the luxury of drilling into my walls and adding ethernet to every room. However, I can utilize the preexisting power lines in the walls. I haven't had a chance to run a speed test, but I was able to stream anything onto my tv up to 4k and stream my PS4 via PSTV which worked as flawlessly as running a cat6 ethernet cable straight from my ethernet switch. However your experience may vary depending on your house's wiring.

Note:
Living in a duplex, apartment, or any other shared housing you run the risk of someone else being able to tap into your private network. I made sure to test if anyone in my complex was already using one, thankfully they weren't. These are best for solitary houses if you're worried about security. Also, a newer built residence is more likely to perform better.

The only reason I'm giving these a 4/5 is because you can only buy these adapters in pairs. I couldn't find anyone selling singles unless they were used.
title: Use the wires your home has already has!

text: I had a Paperwhite before that I loved for reading outdoors or traveling, it's lighter than the Kindle Fire, smaller, and you can read it in the bright sun.  It went to the dentist with me, and when I stood up it slid off my lap onto the tile floor never to awaken again.  My life flashed before my eyes, and after some attempts at reviving the old one, I gave up and quickly ordered another.  I haven't tried the waterproof feature, although I doubt I'll try reading it in the swimming pool.  At least I feel it's protected for accidental moisture exposure.  I haven't had to recharge the battery yet, so can't really make a good judgment on that.  It comes with a USB cord, but not the power/plug part.  If you're like me, you probably have several of those lying around or auxiliary USB connections to use.  My one complaint about this and most other electronic devices, is that none come with even a brief set of instructions.  They all presume prior knowledge and that's just not the case.  The instructions are in the unit, and if you don't know how to use it, they aren't accessible to you.  I'm a person who wants and needs a paper instruction booklet that I can flip through.  Reading it off a screen just doesn't do it, especially if it's on the device.  You can't try out a feature without leaving the information page, and it's not easy to go back and forth.  For those of us that just aren't familiar with the terminology or have access to a millennial to help, you have to access the manual on another device.  Please, technology gods, make paper instructions available with the device or an add on purchase.  Aside from that, I love my Kindles and use them every day.
title: Replacement for previous Kindle PW

This is a nice looking mesh router pair. About the size of a wine bottle box, but not quite as tall, and smooth white. Even if it’s out where people can see it, it not obviously electronics.

The first device (not that there’s one you have to set up before the other, just the one I grabbed first) set up in minutes and was easy to add to my home network and configure. And that becomes the parent node. So if you want your parent node in a specific place, make sure it’s the one you set up first. The second one….not so much. The app wouldn’t see it. Then the app saw it, but it wouldn’t add it to the network. After a lot of fiddling with it when we had the patience, we finally got it on the network. The biggest “are we still in the dark ages of the internet” moment was that when we would hook it up wired, it still insisted on trying to connect wirelessly. I expected it to recognize how it's connected! It’s nice to know that we have not just internet, but fast internet access in the whole house now, whether we’re all the way upstairs, in the back corner of the basement, or standing next to the modem.

Once we finally got it up and going it’s worked fine, you don’t even notice them. And that’s how it’s supposed to be. No drops or lag when you get handed off to a different device. Just seamless. Note that if you are on a wireless device that connects to one of these, and these are hardwired, your modem/service provider router will see the wireless device as connected via hardwire too. If you aren’t seeing your laptop on your WiFi list, look on your hardwired list.

I bought this product as an attachment and and organizer for additional products that I want to connect to my MacBook Pro (two USB-C ports).
PROs:
- Space gray color 'almost' matches the MacBook Pro Space Gray, but it is still off a shade. Nothing to complain about.
- The angled portion that sits under the laptop is a very nice refinement to the other products available. It really stabilizes the other attachments and doesn't "rock" like other adaptors I have used. Nice differentiator that has value.
- There are ample USB-C ports (2) for high speed devices (I use an offline portable drive), three USB 3.0 ports, and an SD and Micro card reader. All seem to work just fine (I've used the USB 3.0 ports, but not the Micro SD or SD ports).
- The adaptor butts up securely to the laptop, and the connector USB-C males fit snuggly into the female USB-C ports in the laptop. The result looks seamless and like an extension to the laptop side.
- Comes with a sleeve to put the adaptor in when traveling, which is an additionally nice touch.
CONs
- I did plug in some old flash sticks, which had difficulty connecting through the USB 3.0 ports. If you hold them tight, or wiggle slightly, they seem to connect and come on line.
- I would have liked one extra USB-C port, and one less USB 3.0 port for my purposes, and because USB-C is becoming prevalent in future products.
Overall, I am happy with the purchase and would recommend the product even though it is more expensive that alternative adaptors.

text:
Let's face it, this is not the greatest tablet out there but it is an excellent value for the money. First the cons: The screen quality and colors are meh but I do appreciate the option to brighten or dim the screen that is right at the top of the screen and can easily be accessed by a down-swipe. This one is my third upgrade so I pretty much know what I'm getting going in and for my purposes, it is just what I need.

So here is what I like about the Fire. It is very easy to use and not at all complicated. Most of the settings you need are at the top of the swipe down screen. You can also use it to surf the web, read and send emails, play games, listen to music, stream on all the apps, Netflix, Hulu, HBO, Showtime, Amazon Prime, of course, etc. There are tons of Apps available and you can access all your social media accounts. I use mine to stream video, read (although it is a bit bulkier than the Kindle reader) books, daily newspapers, and magazines, check the weather. I also love that you can download movies and videos to watch when the internet is not available. For what I use it for, the Fire is perfect, and when I buy it on a deal for $99, it is a bargain. text:
I usually use a three monitor setup at my office, but picked this up for a second monitor to keep in my go bag to set up when working at a customer site. I wanted a screen that was light, sharp and clear, and easy to set up, and picked this up to try.

The screen is sharp and clear. 1080p on a 15" screen is the same pixel density as my laptop. Works fine in either portrait or landscape, no autodetecting so you have to change it in the OS if you want to rotate it. Had a detection issue initially (defaulted to 640x480), but it has been at 1080p since. Good viewing angles, colors stay consistent even viewed quite off center, it claims to be IPS and looks the part.

14.5" wide by 9" tall and 1/2" thick with the case on. Weight is about 2.5lbs also with the case - which you need, as it is the stand as well, but the case is just under 1lb of that. Compares very well to trying to carry a full size monitor. The case is a protective full wraparound, magnetically held in place front and back when on, it is pretty secure from falling off completely, but does not provide any bottom cushioning when vertical in portrait orientation in a bag, so keep that in mind. My laptop bag has some cushioning under the inner, should be fine there.

As a stand, the case does a good job as long as you set it up on a flat surface and have the case on the right way - one side is the inside and is softer, greyish, and grippier, and the other is more black and slick, and if you put it on backwards it looks like it is attached but doesn't work well at all. Confused me for a bit the first time I took the case off and put it back on wrong. Otherwise it is a fairly standard magnetic tablet case / stand. It is ONLY attached by magnets though, so pretty easy to disconnect unintentionally if you are twisting it at all while moving it in the stand position.

Connectivity is primarily USB-C. It has two ports, one is power only, the other is signal or both signal and power. My Latitude E5570 can provide power over the Thunderbolt / USB-C connector using the same cable as the video signal. So just the USB-C to C connector in the bag and quick to connect / disconnect is perfect.

The micro HDMI cable and separate power supply and USB A-C cable for power will be useful a few times a year when traveling for fun and I want to bring this with the xbox - but that won't be a primary use, and holding a controller while staying at the right distance for this to be functional would not be perfect.

It has a speaker. Volume and quality compare poorly to my laptop speakers, this is more of a checkbox feature. I have no plans to use them.

It also comes with a plastic screen protector ready to install. At this size it is nearly impossible to get one of those on without bubbles, and I tried but was unsuccessful in avoiding those. But I don't see any real need for it anyway - the case protects it for travel, and this isn't a touchscreen to carry around, no matter how tablet like it looks.

Overall, it is meeting my need for a travel monitor quite well. We'll see how TSA treats it the next time I hit the air, and how it holds up over time, but this is very good and quite affordable for what I needed today. Only issue is I keep trying to treat it like a touch screen, which it is not, but I'll get used to that in time.

text: My primary A/V system is 15 years old but my plasma TV, amplifier, and surround sound speakers still provide excellent quality. With that said, as I have purchased new input devices, I wound up with a daisy chain of HDMI and optical splitters  behind my television. As my cables and splitters aged I found myself jiggling cables to make good connections. The last straw was the death of my old ROKU and they no longer make one with an optical out. I bought all new cables and the FERRISA 4x2 Matrix, hooked up all my equipment but somethings had sound but no video. I thought  I needed help setting up the EDID switches so I called Amazon support. They have a  very friendly support team, but even with changes to the EDID switches no change. Amazon overnighted a new device because of the holidays coming up. Still no luck, so Amazon asked if I would call the manufacturer for help. Fiibest support was great! We tried some changes to the EDID switches again with no success. They asked me to send them a list of all my input device's resolution and my TV's resolution. My TV is 780P. Some of my peripherals were 780P but newer devices were 1080P. I manually changed everything to 780P. Eureka! Everything worked. (780 & 1080 are both hi def). The Matrix instructions tell you not to leave it turned on all the time so you would have to unplug the jack to power it down. I suggested to Fiibest that they add a power switch. I have slowly turned my house into a "Smart Home" with Amazon Echo devices and I simply set up an Echo outlet. I just have to say "Alexa, turn on TV Matix" and it is done. Long review... bottom line: If you have equipment that is all the same video resolution this switch is plug and play. If you don't it is easy to manually change the resolution in the settings menu of your devices. I'm very pleased with it.

text:
First, the good. This is significantly better than the entry level USG. I had to upgrade as I got a faster internet connection. The smaller model would max out around 200Mbps with most of the features turned off and hardware offload enabled. This model still requires most features disabled, but I'm able to hit 500mbps to 600mbps on it. Turning on the threat management significantly slows the device.

Ubiquiti has a higher end model (XG) that was pulled from the market due to problems for a bit. I'm hoping they get that product back out and also add something in between this PRO model and the XG or bump the specs. A gigabit connection couldn't run on this model and it's obvious that the PRO isn't powerful enough for heavy workloads even at 500Mbps.

I really like the management features on unifi gear and it's the big selling point. It was pretty easy to upgrade from the smaller USG to the pro model also.

I do hope they get a slightly faster model out and consider upgrading to 2.5Gbps nbase-T connectivity so one doesn't have to jump to fiber connections for moderate performance.

If you were using a connection up to say 300Mbps, most of the features would work and you'd be pretty happy with this. I just don't think it's ready for 500Mbps to gigabit speeds.

Finally, the IPv6 support on this device is mediocre. Part of the problem is the upstream router from my cable provider, but the IPv6 supports feels like an afterthought and is a little irritating to try to setup. Documentation is lacking in this area. I can get an IP address on the WAN interface, but have never been able to get it to assign an IP to the inside network. If you need IPv6 functionality, it might be better to go with another product.

text:
I'm a big fan of UAG products they never disappoint. The workmanship on this product was best in class. However, there were two design short comings that are causing some problems.

The first shortcoming is that when I put the case in my bag spine-down, just jostling the bag will cause the keyboard portion to slide towards the hinges which causes it to become "unclipped" from the front of the case which forces me to re-seat the keyboard back into the slot. The remedy for this would be for a second set of clips to be molded into the plastic to ensure a sturdier grip onto the keyboard based.

The second shortcoming probably is more a trade-off than a shortcoming. Although the transparent polycarbonate/acrylic top cover is great looking, it also acts as an insulator and contributes to the display overheating. This is as much a design flaw that Microsoft has been criticized for but if you see yellowing around the edges of the display, overheating is a contributing cause. When I take the cover off the display cools down and does recover. However, from experience I know that means I am shortening the life of the display and all the components inside. I'm willing to live with this trade-off as it is still better to protect the device but when I am using this in desktop mode with the Microsoft docking station at my desk, I always leave a fan to blow on the display. UAG could improve upon this by using an open ribbed approach for the top half of the case allowing for the shell to be in direct contact with air.

All in all, I am satisfied with the product as there has yet to be another like it that performs any better.
title: Good product but some design flaws.

text: I purchased these earbuds in December and I have to say that I am very impressed with the overall sound quality and performance considering the $50 price point. For the money, I don't believe that you can find a better pair of wireless earbuds in terms of sound reproduction, fit, and overall quality. Sure, I could have paid more for Apple earbuds but the marginal increase in performance is not worth the extra cost. The pairing is simple, steady, and reliable. Battery life is about 3 hours on a single charge when I listen to music, which is on par with other earbuds and what I'd expect from a device that I wear at the gym and for short periods of time. Midrange and highs are good (letter grade = B+), but overall bass performance is decent (letter grade B-) which really is as expected. I am not sure how you can engineer solid bass performance into an earbud, so my expectations are modest and given that, the Anker product is a success. My thoughts on overall sound quality are not curved to reflect earbuds as a class, but rather what this device sounds like in reference to any audio reproduction. I have sampled Beats and Apple earbuds and honestly, none of them can replace true over the ear headphones, but that is not their intended purpose just as earphones cannot replicate the sound of reference speakers.  Calls are clear and the microphones do a great job reducing background noise (letter grade = A-). In short - I strongly recommend this product and don't believe that anyone would have any reason to be disappointed with the purchase of this product. In short - This is an excellent product with very good sound,  solid build, easy Bluetooth pairing, comfortable to wear, and nice quality. You could pay more, but why?
title: Excellent Performance at a fantastic price point

text:
At this price point, you can't find a better laptop. I actually recommended this laptop to my sister, and seeing how well it functioned got me to buy one. The combination of processor, build quality, and features make this laptop an incredible value. The Flex 14 does have some downsides, like the ips screen which has an okay contrast ratio and poor color saturation. But that's really it. The keyboard is very comfortable, the trackpad feels quite nice, the pen works incredibly well, the folding feature is intuitive and works well, the battery has okay longevity, and more importantly, charges very quickly with the compact included charger. This new laptop and its charger combined weigh a pound less than my last laptop.
For performance, at stock settings, the ryzen 5 3500u is relatively unimpressive. It's moderately slower than the Intel cpu, and a bit more power efficient. However, in use, I noticed that the fans stay incredibly quiet, and that the chip itself never goes above 65° in synthetic load. So, by tweaking the power limits up a bit, I was able to increase the fan speed, get core temps up to 75°, and boost multicore CPU performance by 40%. This also improved gpu performance by 15%. With this tweak, the Flex 14 is unbeatable. This laptop easily performs well into the $1000 price range, and I recommend it to any college student. If you want a small, light laptop, need to use productivity applications, and you want to play some older games, this is the best laptop you can get for less than $1000.
title: Unbeatable

text:
I did some very thorough research online and some adventuring in stores, and I have confirmed the following:

Samsung HDTV models listed below require an "M8 - 1.25 x 43mm" bolt in the bottom two screw holes, which does not really exist outside of the internet and cannot be found in hardware stores. Even the online resellers that are stating they sell 43mm bolts are actually 45mm and are just using false advertisement.

Alternatively, you can go to a hardware store and use the slightly more popular "M8 - 1.25 x 45mm" bolt with very minor space between the Part F bracket and the TV back and still have a solid connection without issue, which is what I have done. You can add a washer or two and the connection should be really solid. I found my bolts at a LOWE'S store, and they were the only ones available. I also tried Home Depot and ACE Hardware, who had nothing.

If absolutely necessary and people cannot find either of these bolts, the "M8 - 1.25 x 50mm" size is almost just as comfortable of a fit as the 45mm, though now you have to expect a bit more wobble, unless you want to add about 6 washers.

When I went to LOWE'S, one of the employees there had created a list of TV models by Samsung that he's run into that require these bolts. He pulled out the paper and read it off and showed me. He explained all of the issues I have mentioned here - that there is no such thing as a 43mm bolt, unless it's custom made online somewhere, or if you cut the bolt yourself to size(which would be easier to do if you start with a 50mm bolt). He also explained how people were being scammed on Amazon by people selling 43mm bolts but they were actually 45mm. I took a photo of his list and wrote down all supported models in it. I was also notified that it is nearly impossible to find the 45mm bolts in a store without it being a hex-top bolt, so you'll need a socket wrench to install the bolts into the TV if you're lucky enough to find them in a store. Otherwise, people can go online and grab them on Amazon. They're more expensive on Amazon though by a few dollars. They're only a few cents in stores. After reading many reviews, I've discovered that LOWE'S and ACE Hardware seem to be the best stores to find these bolts.

Here's the list of Samsung HDTV models requiring the 43mm-45mm bolts:
-- D6000
-- D6400
-- D6450
-- D6500
-- D6900
-- MU8500
-- NU6070
-- NU6900
-- NU7100
-- KS8000
-- NU8000
-- MU8000
-- RU7100
-- RU8000
-- Q6 (Q6FN/Q6/Q6F)
-- Q8 (Q8FN/Q8/Q8F)
-- Q60 (Q60/Q60R)
-- Q70 (Q70/Q70R)
-- Q80 (Q80/Q80R)

You need to please add this information in the description of your mount stand. Mention that you do not provide the two bottom bolts necessary for these Samsung models. However, I have a better idea - why not upgrade your mount stand product by adding 45mm M8 bolts in it. Make a newer version. That will make your product even more valuable to costumers looking for a mount. If they see a description like that, their reaction would be similar to, "Wow! This product swivels, tilts, has height adjustment, AND has Samsung support right out of the box! Amazing!" then you'll only receive more success. I'll be honest, your product is REALLY good. I couldn't be happier, but the headache of searching these bolts out are insane, and cost way too much on Amazon. We're talking $6.15 - $15.00 for these bolts, when they are only worth about 97 cents a pop in store. Just update your product to a new model that included the M8 45mm bolt with washers and add an extra $6.00 to the cost of purchase. You'll only succeed further with this great product because you'll be giving hope to everyone that owns a Samsung these days!

Just a note for anyone unaware, "M8" basically stands for the width size of 1.25mm, while the other sizes (43, 45, 50, etc.) are bolt lengths. No matter what someone buys, they need an M8, but with the confusion involved in the length sizing, it's basically whatever decision you decide to make. 

TLDR; 
If you have a Samsung, you need "M8 - 1.25 x 45mm" bolts.
title: Samsung Owners, You NEED to buy M8 - 1.25 x 45mm Bolts for the Product! Please Read!

text:
My son's old tablet was in serious need of an upgrade. I wasn't sure whether to go with a new Fire 7 or 8. On Black Friday, the Fire 7 was on a super duper sale, so I decided to go for it and figured it couldn't be THAT much different from a Fire 8. Well, I was quite WRONG!

We gave my son the Fire 7 for Christmas, and he was so excited. Until we quickly had problems with the internet connection holding, although we have great signal here. He tried to download a couple games, that ended up freezing up before they would load. Once he finally got one game going, it would suddenly freeze during game play and shut off. Searching the internet on it was so incredibly slow. Opening apps on it was so incredibly slow. It struggled to even open the Settings menu.

For anyone that wants a tablet for playing games, streaming shows or music, or for using the internet -- the Fire 8 is the WAY TO GO! We returned the 7 and paid the extra $ for the 8, and it was worth every penny. It downloads quickly, plays games smoothly and doesn't act bogged down at all. It's quick and responsive in every way. What a difference!

For anyone that just wants a simple tablet to mainly use as a kindle for reading, or very light internet use - the Fire 7 would be great. OR maybe for a small child that only has a few simple games to play. The value of the 7, mostly if you can get it on sale, is there. But remember it's quite limited in what it can do and the speed it operates.

Because I've actually worked with products made by this company before, though, I was comfortable that things will work out just fine. It seems that I was very wrong. :-(
Upon connecting this device to my computer the first thing that I noticed and concerned me is that I did not get the typical "plug-and-play" reaction that we have come to expect. Secondly, the device listed as a USB PNP device and not a Bluetooth device. Okay, I thought this was weird. Also, but most importantly, it never asked me to install any "drivers" from my Windows PC.
Well, sure enough, I supposedly successfully paired my headphones with this device but no sound.
This morning I called my computer technical support, it turns out, he says, that this device only works on Windows PCs that already have Bluetooth technology on board.
Wow, nothing written on the product description page would have led me to conclude that. Maybe I'm dumb but I don't think so. Bottom line, TREAD CAREFULLY IN LESS YOU KNOW EXACTLY WHAT YOU WANT! :-)

text:
When I bought these headphones, I bought them because I wanted a good stereo headset with good headphones that also had a boom mic for dictation. When I opened the box I was very impressed and pleased with my purchase. I was pleased with my purchase until I put these headphones on my head. :-( :-( I was stunned by their apparent weight. These suckers are heavy. Within minutes, and I mean minutes it felt like someone had strapped rocks to my ears! Wow. Admittedly I do have a physical disability. However, as part of the work that I do, I wear some kind of headphones or headset for the better part of the day at least 3 days a week, often more than that. I know what all kinds of different headphones and headsets feel like, & these are HEAVY! In a very short amount of time, I had the feeling I couldn't or shouldn't hold my head erect. I was amazed in a very negative way. I've also felt headsets that feel like feathers on my head.
Besides all of that, if that's not enough these were very difficult to physically pair with my Bluetooth devices. text:
I bought a new Samsung 970 EVO M.2 NVMe drive and wanted to install it in my older Asus motherboard. I was already using an M.2 drive but it was a SATA drive. I found out that my motherboard would not support the NVMe drive and I needed a way to get it on the PCIe bus.

This little card has done that for me. The card came with two plates. (full size and half size) It came disassembled but they do provide the screws. They also provided a small Phillips screwdriver to assemble it with.

I am still running Windows 7 so I needed a driver from Samsung to get the drive to work. (no drivers specific to the card itself are needed) Before I installed the drivers, Windows attempted to install them and failed. I had an unknown PCI Express device in Device Manager.

After I installed the drivers, everything worked great. I used the data migration software from Samsung and copied my C: drive from my old 2.5" SATA SDD to this new super-fast NVMe drive. It took less than 15 minutes to copy my 500GB of data on my boot drive.

I went to the BIOS and told it to boot from the Samsung 970 EVO and it has been working great ever since. (just set it up today)

I ran a few CrystalDiskMark benchmarks on the drive. and I get different results than other people are getting. I actually got much faster results on the 4K QD32 tests but slower on the sequential read and write tests.

The Samsung Magician software told a different story than the CrystalDiskMark software. It had the sequential reads at 3600MB per second. (what I would expect from the drive)

I am sharing the PCIe bus with a video card so even though I put the card in 16x slot, I believe it is running at 8x since the video card is in the other 16x slot. Either way, it is screaming fast. My computer boots much faster and games and programs load incredibly fast. Photoshop loads so fast, it is like opening a browser. Photoshop is up and usable in about 4 seconds. (older CS version) Outlook loads in about 1.5 seconds.

The card can hold two M.2 drives. (one B key and one M key) I do not know if you can use them both at the same time or not.

I didn't bother with the heatsink, thermal material or the rubber bands. I ran the Samsung Magician software many times after lots of disk activity to monitor the temp. It is right where it should be without any heatsink. I have installed several of these drives right on the motherboard and I have never used any type of heatsink in the past.

I do not believe that Samsung recommends using anything on the drive but other manufacturers may. There is an LED light that goes from white, red, green, blue and then eventually back to white. I'm not sure why it does this but it could just be for decoration. (It did say RGB in the description) There is a second LED that is always red and shows disk activity.

The price is great, it is easy to set up and use and comes with cooling options if you choose to use them.
title: Inexpensive and works well.  Easy to install.  I did not use the heatsink.

Build quality on these headphones is a mixed bag. The cable it comes with is replaceable, and is nicely thick and braided, which inspires confidence. The headphones themselves, though, are made of a really light hollow feeling plastic, and the adjustment feels really stiff and gritty. The foam padding on the ear cups is also quite firm and uncomfortable even after just a couple minutes of listening- especially as these are on-ear, not over-ear.

Sound quality is surprisingly good for $11- highs are fairly clear and detailed, bass has decent power but lacks a ton of clarity, and the mids are kinda lost in between the two. The overall sound profile makes these good for heavier music like rock and metal, but might not work for everyone's taste. For the price, though, it's hard to nitpick too hard.
title: Okay Budget Headphones

text:
As listening headphones, these are great. Build quality is solid, padding in nice and gentle for extended listening periods, and the buttons are nice and tactile.

Sound quality is pretty good, if a bit soft. Highs are nice and clear, mids are a little lacking, and bass is really empty. Generally I'd say it's an energetic kind of sound, but it feels a little flat and hollow. That's not necessarily a terrible thing, this makes for far more pleasant listening than the really warm bass heavy drivers you typically get in cheaper headphones, but it does mean that for heavier genres like rock or metal, you might find your music sounding a bit anemic.

The ANC is where these headphones fall apart. Just don't flip that switch, don't bother. The sealed closed back design works well enough for sound isolation, and IMO turning on the ANC actually enhances the noise rather than removes it. I tested sitting in a room next to a standing fan- a constant tone. The ANC turned that tone in a loud digital warble that made the noise much more annoying and harsh on the ears. At normal listening volumes the design of the earcups alone killed most of the background noise anyway.
title: Nice Wireless Headphones- Terrible Active Noise Cancellation.

text:
Much like its wired-only sibling, these headphones out of the box seem small and flimsy, but build quality is actually not terrible. You're not expecting much, but the aesthetics are high quality, and it feels good enough to wear- so long as you realise the cups are small enough that they're on-ear, not over-ear.

What you get extra with the "Pro" version is of course bluetooth capability, as well as a surprisingly nice padded mesh carry bag.

Sound quality on this one is perhaps slightly worse than the wired-only Impulse headphones, with a sound signature that is a touch more bass heavy than even those were, and is a bit congested sounding, lacking clarity in the mids which can make the vocals indistinct at times. Still, for the price these hold up very well.

Considering how slim the price difference is between these and the wired-only Impulse headphones, I'd say that go for these "Pro" headphones is basically a no-brainer if you're on a budget and can't afford anything in the next tier of quality.
title: Surprisingly Good for the Price

text:
Out of the box, my first reaction was "oh wow, these are the tiniest flimsiest children's headphones I've seen". In the hands, the build quality isn't quite that bad, but it's not spectacular. For the price, you can't expect much, and you don't get much. The thinnest bare minimum "padding" on the top strap, some memory foam cups that are so small they sit on the ears, not over them, and wire friction adjustable mounts.

Sound quality is surprisingly good despite price and appearance though. The sound is a bit warm, heavy in the bass, but is still fairly clear and holds up shockingly well in the mids and highs. text:
As a disclaimer, despite looking like a neck pillow, this is certainly not designed to be soft and comforting for a nap. However, I find this to be an interesting form factor for getting big sound and keeping your hands free. Earbuds can be fatiguing inside the ears for long periods of time, closed back headphones can be sweaty and fatiguing, open backs are better, but you still have a floppy thing that may or may not clamp onto your head well and can get in the way of you hearing the world. The tradeoff with these of course is that everyone else can hear what you're listening to, but there's no fatigue wearing these all day at home, doing chores, working at a desk, etc...

The sound quality is- interesting. Because you essentially have a soundbar strapped to your neck, you get a big wide soundstage that gives you a lot of surround sound depth. However, you also lose the benefits of earbuds and headphones that seal around the ear and give you stronger bass. The overall effect is sound that's good, but loses a bit of clarity and depth. For someone who isn't a serious audiophile, I don't think this would be a big issue at all.

The only other consideration with sound is that of course unlike headphones, the speakers on these won't follow your head. This means that as you look around, the sound doesn't track with you, so your head kinda turns and floats through the surround sound. This can take a little while to get used to, and can be distracting at times, but after a while really isn't a big deal at all.
title: Unique Formfactor, Works Surprisingly Well

text:
This is a cute little throwback novelty- the manages to be a surprisingly good modern device as well! The build quality feels excellent and gives a great vintage/steampunk look with the bright glowing dial. The dials are smooth, and the setting switch has nice distinctive clicks as you toggle modes.

The sound quality is also surprisingly good. Past half volume you do get a bit of distortion, but the speaker on this guy is shockingly loud when you try to push it. At more reasonable volumes it's god a decent sound that's perhaps a little muddy in the lows, but is still totally pleasant for general listening.

As a gift this is an excellent little novelty, because its also perfectly functional as well!
title: Adorable and Decent Sounding

text:
Build quality is nothing special- mostly plastic, with decently soft padded cushions. In longer listening sessions it gets a little warm, but overall feels fine on the head. There's not a ton of adjustment and they're a bit loose on my head, so these are definitely casual listening headphones, not for active uses.

The controls are nice clicky tactile buttons- single presses skip tracks forward and back, whereas holding for a few seconds will adjust the volume up and down. Simple, but effective. O also appreciated the inclusion of a 3.5mm jack and cable, meaning you can still connect directly to these from a device that still has a headphone jack, or something that doesn't have bluetooth.

Sound quality is alright, but muddy. Highs are decently clear, mids are muffled, and lows have a bit of thump but with very little definition. Overall effect is it sounds a bit like you have cotton in your ears.

For the price, these aren't the worst, but they wouldn't be my first choice either.

The product was easy to set up and get the drives formatted and configured. This is my second NAS device but I’m far from an expert in configuring a device like this.

First - the multimedia application the instructions tell you to download is not available and they do not reference what app replaces it in the instructions.

Second - I downloaded the multimedia app that replaced the one in the instructions and configured shared folder permissions. I downloaded the app for my iPhone and was able to find the device on the network. HOWEVER, the app constantly disconnects even after triple checking all the shared folder permissions. It is unbelievably annoying. The app has the multimedia server “enabled” when you look at the settings on your computer but the app shows it is not enabled on my phone with no option to enable it within the phone app even though I had admin rights.

Third - the videos in the multimedia folder can be watched (assuming the app doesn’t disconnect me BUT, there’s no audio. Out of the blue it worked for about a half hour after reinstalling the multimedia app but then...poof, no audio again and I have no idea why.

The main reason I bought this was to have access for myself and my wife to all our photos and videos. It’s a huge disappointment right now. The manufacturer website support is nearly nonexistent as well.

I’m sure I can’t return the hard drives I bought for this. Between this device and the hard drives I’m over $700.00 invested and feel like it’s a giant waste of money at this point. I will happily update this review if something changes and it works.

It could be user error on some level but I have tried every conceivable thing and I truly believe their mobile app is garbage.

UPDATE - I can connect to this device as a server with my Mac and access it like a normal drive which is fantastic. However, with my PC I am not able to connect to it following the instructions provided within the app interface (through a browser).

text:
What a shame Anker. Why make a device you know will begin to decline right outside of the warranty?

I have owned the speaker for 33 months and it is literally unusable. We began needing to keep it plugged in constantly at about 24 months, with battery life markedly reduced at about 18 months. We routinely maintained the batteries by fully charging, disconnecting and running the unit down.

Why make a product that needs to be thrown in the trash in a little over 2 years? Do you make disposable products? I expect to purchase audio equipment that sounds great and lasts and will not simply die in about two years. That's correct, you cannot replace the batteries or just plug it into the wall, it's dead.

Lastly, I contacted customer service and they were completely disinclined to help replace the unit. They stated "Know that we register all defects and evaluate them statistically. These statistics enable us to identify increased defect rates or concentrated product issues, so thank you for letting us know about this." This means they are probably very aware of the battery life issue and apparently find it acceptable to make products with complex components and electronics that you throw away and they also do not care that you need to replace it.

In an era of social and environmental awareness, this is shameful.

Buy a different speaker.
title: Buyer Beware & What a Shame

text:
Ok I’m not a highly knowledgeable person when it comes to tech, but I’m not a novice either. I actually bought the Show 8 and the Google Nest Hub at the same time because they were priced the same. I figured I would keep the better of the two. Nest arrived first so I set it up first. Setup was incredibly easy (I already have a nest mini), eventually easier than the Show. I also have a gmail account so that speeds up things on the Nest as well. I wasn’t keeping my photos on Google but it was pretty quick to add favorites in one folder and the Nest is now a digital photo frame. I have it on my nightstand because when you turn out the lights it really does go dark as well with a hint of the time showing - in full screen size. I am VERY sensitive to light at night and this doesn’t bother me at all. I also really like the “good morning” routine that you set up in the Nest better than the Show. It’s simple enough to ask and get info right before walking out the door.
Once the Show arrived I did the setup thinking it would be easy as I have 3 dots and an Echo already. So yeah, setup went ok until you explore thinking ALL the reviews are wrong and you CAN turn off the “try this” feature. The answer is NO, you can’t. I have every part that should turn it off switched to off (even on the app). Constant “try this” on the screen. It’s ALWAYS there. And there is a list of what seems like a 100 “cards” so it never runs out. The software must’ve changed because all of the offered suggestions to turn it off aren’t accurate for what is currently possible. If you don’t care about that/wouldn’t bother you, then choose the unit that dominates your home or the website you use the most.
So which is better? Meh, they’re about the same IMO. My sons and I usually have them compete with each other to see which one can answer a question accurately or with the best info. Lately there’s no clear winner on that, but Google is usually easier to understand. The Show does NOT go completely dark at night so I could never have it on my nightstand and the clock is never full screen so that’s annoying too. I have added a seasonal photo image on my amazon photo account using a computer so it’s decorative in the living room. I’m going to be installing a video doorbell myself soon and some interior cameras so I’ll update my review when those gadgets are added to compare use. Reviews I’ve read online say both units will work fine on both the doorbell and cameras so I’ll to do the installation to judge it.
title: Show vs Nest - I now have both

text:
When I recently took inventory of my battery stash, I thought there had to be a better way. As you can see from my photo, I had various types and sizes of packaging all tossed in a kitchen drawer. It was a mess. There must be a better way to store these. And there is. Apparently, battery cases are a thing.

Of course when I started looking at options, I wanted explosion proof and water resistance. However after looking at dozens of cases, I realized, where are everyone’s D batteries? The vast majority of the battery cases had six slots, max, for D batteries. What? I have a camping lantern and fan that each take four D batteries. And what about the 9Vs? I buy those by the dozen. When one fire alarm starts chirping, you better have a whole lot of 9Vs.

So I got this case. I need usability more than I need explosion proofing. It still doesn’t have enough 9V storage, but I can use extra D and C compartments for those (see photo).

I also wanted one with a pocket for my button batteries. This has slots, but I’d prefer to keep them packaged as I have various types. The only reason I deducted 1 Star was because the pocket is not tight, nor does it have a closure. The handle to carry this case is on the hinge side which becomes the top when carrying the case. This means that the pocket is upside down when you pick up the case. In my use, this led to button batteries falling out when I unzipped the case as they had fallen out of the pocket. It would be great if the pocket held them in. I solved this but putting all my button batteries inside a large ziplock bag and then inside the pocket. This way, the tiny packages don’t fall out.

I like this case. Now my batteries are easily accessible in the pantry. There is now a ton of free room in my kitchen drawer. Also, I can easily take stock of what sizes I’m running low on.

Oh and obviously, the tester is a huge bonus. I have a tornado shelter where I keep cases of batteries for emergencies, not to be used around the house. It’ll be nice to go test them before each tornado season to see if they’ve outlived their life and need replacing.
title: Neat and tidy solution to save your junk drawer.

text:
This panoramic camera mount is well made for the price point and my rating would be five stars if it were not for the fact that it is almost unusable until you disassemble the entire product and remove all the friction grease that is covering it. If you don't, your hands, camera, camera bag, and anything else this product comes in contact with will be covered in sticky goo that simply will not come off with soap and water. Normally this type of grease would be a good thing, but the grease is not contained within the product, but instead coating parts you will frequently touch. This means that no matter how careful you are, you will get it everywhere.

I ended up taking everything apart and giving it a good cleaning, removing all of the goo, and making the mount usable.

Here is what I did:

1. Find the end of both rails that contain a small set screw that prevents the rail from sliding all the way out.
2. Use a small blade or screwdriver to peel back a little of the rubber pad directly over the set screw enough so you can access it.
3. Use a 1.5mm hex key to back out the set screw until the rail slides out of the mount.
4. Use a 3mm hex key to carefully remove the hex bolt that allows the upper rail to pivot.
5. Take both rails and mounting blocks and spway them with WD-40. WD-40 acts as a solvent for this type of grease.
6. Use a toothbrush to clean the teeth on the rails and also the gears in the mounting blocks.
7. Wipe the excess WD-40 off with a paper towel.
8. Gently wash the rails and blocks in water and dawn dish soap which will remove the WD-40.
9. Thoroughly dry the parts.
10. Reassemble the parts in reverse order.

I ended up using applying some PTFE lubricant which is dry, not sticky and won't attract dirt.
title: Great Once You Remove The Sticky Friction Grease

I received this as a gift for Christmas, so keep in mind that I’ve been using this just a short time. I may update if any issues arise. But so far: I love it. I didn’t need or want a full on smart watch, but wanted a slight upgrade from an old Fitbit I had that didn’t even have a watch on it, and sometimes needed charged twice a day. I wanted a regular watch with maybe a few bonus features-I had used a pebble for awhile and it was perfect but even with the rebble software it was no longer synching with my phone, and pebble no longer exists as a company. This fits the bill perfectly for what I wanted. The heart rate is fairly accurate (as compared to my own measurement taken), the steps are pretty similar to what my Fitbit measured, and sleep is I’m sure as accurate as such a device can be, and the stress tracking is interesting as well. The face is a bit bigger than I thought it would be when I added it to my Christmas list but it’s growing on me. I was irritated that every time I looked at the watch face the arms would move to 10:10 (so the arms are out of the way of the digital display)but I figured out how to change that to only move when I tap the screen. Oh and I got this Christmas Day and I have yet to need to charge it almost a week later, if I was using the digital display more I imagine I would need to charge more often.
Overall: if you want a regular, nice looking watch with some cool tracking features, this is for you. If you want a feature-laden smart watch, this isn’t it.
title: A nice watch with some bonus features, not a smartwatch

text:
This is probably one of the best AIO coolers I have ever installed in a computer system. I would highly recommend this for anyone looking to get their temps under control. I am primarily a workstation, coding, multi-VM, type of power user, who happens to play games every once in a while. Water cooling is not just for gaming and is a powerful component to have for any type of user, so don't let such a simple misconception keep you from enjoying prolonged component life and quieter system operation. There are a few key things to watch out for though:

1) This matters more for those who will mount the radiator at the front of their case: When measuring your setup to determine whether the rubber hoses are long enough, do not take a linear measurement from the area in your case where the radiator will go over to the CPU. The rubber hoses are thick and the way they are mounted with a 90 degree elbow at the CPU bracket do not let them lay very flat, they maintain a rather rigid curve to the radiator. Instead, measure more in a half moon shape from the radiator area over to the CPU. This will give you a better idea if you are going to have enough length to work with. If you happen to be mounting this on the rear or top of the case where the radiator is in closer proximity to the CPU, you shouldn't have anything to worry about.

2) When you first turn this on, do not be surprised if there is a lot of noise coming from the motor in the CPU block, including vibrations, gurgling, bubbling, gremlins, gnomes, or other unnatural sounds that may come from it. During shipping there is no telling how many bubbles have been spread throughout the hoses, radiator, and CPU block. As long as it sounds like something is moving in there, let it run for several minutes. It took about 5 minutes before the pump on my system had managed to cycle enough fluid to situate all of the air bubbles where they belong, and the system went dead quiet as soon as it did. It hasn't made a peep since and has been running silent and flawless for days. If you are concerned about thermal damage to the processor, remove the RAM from your motherboard so it fails to POST but still maintains power to accessory fans. This will allow you to clear the system without putting any actual thermal stress on the CPU. If you're still nervous after the bubbling sounds go away, boot to BIOS and watch your CPU temps from there for a few more minutes to make sure everything looks good.

3) The CPU block comes with some thermal compound already installed and ready to go, which is great if you so happened to forget to buy any before wanting to install this kit. So right out of the box, this is ready to go which I thought was quite nice but not clearly advertised anywhere. Now, for those who intend to use this for more high-end processors, heavy gaming, overclocking, etc then I might suggest having an extra plastic scraper handy and scraping this off the copper block so you can cleanly place your own desired thermal cooling paste of choice (Arctic, Deepcool, Grizzly, etc.) on instead.

4) It doesn't take a super nerd or computer genius to install this, though they may be able to complete the process faster. If you take your time and go slow, just about anyone can do this on their first try without issues. When in doubt, check out Google or YouTube - there are tons of walk through videos for installing AIO (including this exact one) which cover just about any question you could possibly have.
title: Excellent Entry Level Water Cooling at Reasonable Price

text:
I'm an experienced puzzler solver and while this brand of puzzle has a beautiful colorful picture, it has some frustrating drawbacks. The thickness of the puzzle backing is thin compared to the German made puzzles that I enjoy working with. Another issue is the glossiness of the pieces make it very difficult to see the images of each piece if sitting down because of the glare from overhead or even window lighting. One is "forced" to stand and look down on the pieces to see the image parts clearly. Tough on the back after hours of work. And finally, the pieces do not fit tightly or "snap" into place. This puzzle's image is very detailed with fine and tiny lines which is good for those who build puzzles for the challenge but because the fittings are not tight, its easy to make placement errors. 24 hours of construction time and not quite half done which indicates the difficulty level. One must have patience with this puzzle.

UPdate: iF YOU WANT A CHALLENGE, THIS IS A GREAT PUZZLE. 98% of the pieces have the same basic shape, 2 knobs and 2 cut outs. I competed this puzzle in 60 hours. The difficulty level comes from the fat the puzzles is large with very intricate details but the photos on the front and bottom of the box are not clear enough to show the delays. One needs a strong magnifying lens to study the details. The other hindrance is the high gloss finish. It hard to get proper lighting shining on the workstation so the pieces can be seen while sitting. Standing directly over the puzzle is necessary.
Now that its done, I'll frame and hang it in my puzzles gallery.
Good luck to all who attempt this puzzle.
title: Beautiful but.....

text:
This is our first foray into mesh Wi-Fi and I've got to say we're pretty impressed with this entry-level, three-pack setup.

Fed up with the old wall-plug extenders – both with and without external antennas – we have used with disappointing results over the years, we decided to give this system a go in my mother's 2,500 square foot, two-story house that has partial Austin limestone walls throughout the ground floor.

Working from home, we must have reliable internet everywhere we go and – only a day or so into it – we're pleased so far.

I will say that the signal has ebbed and flowed sometimes but there are so many variables and multiple devices that can make that happen and I've been too preoccupied to experiment with running speed tests and repositioning the cube(s), which are not unattractive. Perhaps the newer model might yield better results under our circumstances.

This system does require one to use iOS or Android apps for setup, so if you're still using a flip phone (as my 82-year-old mother is) you'll need to find another solution or get a neighbor kid to come help. The process is no more or less difficult than setting up an Alexa or AirTV device, which could be a bit challenging for some.

Bottom line: now, we can work and satisfactorily stream all over the house so I'm a happy camper, especially given the price point.
title: 3-Pack: Pretty pleased so far in 2-Story, 2500 sf house w/stone walls

text:
I knew in purchasing the laptop I'd need to make immediate upgrades. I didn't need the best processor as all my work is done online, but do open multiple taps and email all day long. I added 8 gb RAM and 500 gb SSD, which should be plenty for me, so overall $80 in upgrades that add to the cost of the laptop. Still cheaper than a stronger processor laptop that I'd pay $100+ more for and still end up upgrading memory and storage. Boot time is lightning fast and so far everything responds as it should during work. Upgrading was super easy. There is a space for an extra hard drive, but no connector or caddy so those will have to be purchased separately, adding on another $20 to the cost. If you have a hard time finding the right connector and caddy to fit, I purchased the https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07PDZ4DGF/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1, which ended up fitting fine but the screws are loose holding the drive to the caddy and it is only friction holding it in place in the empty hard drive slot. It is a good tight fit so it is fine for my use, which is mostly work at home, very rarely taking my laptop out of the home to work away. Overall I spent around $450 for a decent processor and plenty of memory and storage.

I'm not sure how the screen would do in a real world setting. It is fine at home where I can keep it angled correctly on my desk, the keyboard has a good feel to it, not cramped and I'm hitting the right keys so the layout is what I'm used to on my Logitech home keyboard. Mouse pad so far is responsive, which can be a problem in most of my previous laptops. I like the fingerprint reader, which makes starting up that much quicker. Easy to switch out of S-mode. I used last night off the charger for the first time and I forgot to check the time on the battery, but it was not impressive. The laptop itself is nice and lightweight so carrying it my laptop bag shouldn't be cumbersome.

Overall I am happy with my purchase and would recommend this laptop with the upgrades noted above. Would not recommend unless you are planning on upgrading. It worked fine before the SSD upgrade (upgraded memory right out of the box), but once you start saving anything you'll quickly run out of room leaving no room for temporary files on your primary drive. At the very least you'll need to add a 250 GB drive if you want to store anything on your hard drive.
title: Great laptop for the price.

text:
I received this 10th Generation Kindle as a Christmas present to replace my old 5th generation version. I enjoy reading but I also enjoy playing word games which I did on the old version. All my books are available to this new device from the Cloud. This new pad, as I come to find out however, is ONLY A READER. Only after spending nearly 3 hours on the phone with the great people at Kindle Support I came to find out that none of the games I enjoyed on my old pad are compatible with this "new" 10 Generation device. REALLY?? Who would make a device purporting to encompass new technology that isn’t backward compatible with older generation programs? I’m at a loss to understand this logic. Even Kindle Support wasn’t aware of this non-compatibility - they were also surprised. I AM HIGHLY DISAPPOINTED! Lastly, there doesn’t seem to be any word-game programs for the “NEW" generation device. Mind boggling.

As a reader, it’s very nice. It’s certainly small and lightweight. I like the available cover which turns on the device when it’s opened; no more button to push to awaken it. The backlighting is great compared to my 5th generation Kindle which has a flip-out light built into the case and is powered by the Kindle battery. The touch screen is very sensitive, almost too sensitive but I’ll get used to it. The battery life is so-so; certainly not better that my old one....which I expected it to be. This new device is waterproof - great if I am less careful with it than I am with my phone or if I intend to read under water (lipstick on a pig). The dictionary function is OK, no better or worse than before, just different in design. Seems to me like change for the sake if change so it can be said it’s been "improved ". I have found that the Typo Notification function is better...this I use more than should be required. Apparently, proof reading is a lost art.

So, all that said, I now have a new "reader" and an old word game device. To readers of this review: Forewarned is Forearmed. Just be aware.

text: At first, I balked at a $100 faceplate.  But there's more to it that it would seem.  You remove a sticker from the bottom from the bottom of the CloudKey Gen 2 Plus (in my case, but it works with the non-plus as well), which exposes a set of contacts.  Then, turn of the CloudKey upside down and insert it into the back of the faceplate.  The Ethernet and status light are then remoted to the faceplate and the the CLoudKey knows it is plugged into the faceplate and flips its screen upside down so it is right side up when viewing through the faceplate.  The whole thing is really slick and well worth the price.

text: Let me start by saying that I have 940/35 mbit cable internet and this gateway can handle it (basically wirespeed) with no trouble at all.  And I have DPI enabled, am running all 4 of my security cameras through the gateway (to facilitate having the cameras on their own VLAN and using the gateway's firewall to only permit the appropriate ports to the CloudKey Gen 2 Plus).  And I have a bunch of firewall rules separating the various VLANs.  The important part to understand is that all of that is handled in hardware (offload).  So for my application, it's brilliant.  But if you want to do anything that disables hardware offload such as IPT/Threat management, you won't be able to get much above maybe 200 mbit if that (have not tested myself).  But again, depends on your application. If you had, say, 100mbit internet connectivity and would never upgrade, this device would probably work for you.  The integration with the UNIFI controller and the entire Unifi suite is really nice.
title: Fantastic gateway as long as you understand its limitations

text:
I bought this for home use, mostly for backup. The company I work for has the services of a large IT company who uses QNAP all the time for their business customers. Our service agent recommended I buy the QNAP and I trust him as he has a very high level of expertise.

You have to buy your own drives. I decided to equip with 2 Seagate Ironhorse 6 TB drives using 1 as a Raid 1. Reason is the 6 TB are 7200 RPM (speed). In retrospect I might have gone larger drives. I am sure 6 TB is fine for the next could of years, but when setting up I followed some you tube videos and it was suggested if I want to use for store a home video camera security system later I should partition to leave a couple TB for that system. 6 TB starts at something like 5.6 TB (I guess some is used for the operating system, etc.) so I just left 1.5 TB for the camera system (I have not even bought one yet, just thinking I might).

Setup is easy only if you watch the you-tube videos. If not, you are going to do something wrong for sure. Those are provided by an independent reviewer, who thankfully is extremely knowledgeable. Otherwise you will not have a clue if you are a newbie like me to NAS. In fact, watch them before you buy a NAS. Currently you will be able to find the you-tube I used as is part of a series of several that show you all the features and how to set them up for this model TS-251B-4G. (should be near same for other models).

To make my system as fast as possible I am using Cat 8 cable in my network. I have GB internet also. My main computer is directly connected to the network. I have to say, backing up to this NAS was actually faster than using a USB attached drive that I had been using (USB 3.1).

One feature I set up right away was adding windows, MAC and Linux operating (which may be why I used so much of the hard drive?) Reason is I will give each of the family members a space of their own (as users) and you can backup anything from a computer to your phone. Half my family, which is large, have iphones or ipads. I use windows and android. This supports them all.
title: Seems very fast on my network

text: The Echo Dot 3 is an attractive, compact device. It's a decent speaker with good, clear sound. Where it falls short is where you need it most. 1) Alexa's voice is WAY TOO LOUD! More often than not I find myself just unplugging at night to avoid the temptation to speak the wake word and have her blurt out at high volume like some drunk girl at a party that's already wound down. As it is dependent on wifi, any command while not connected will prompt a super loud reply, like say volume down while using the bluetooth function to stream shows or music. Same for when it connects to a device. She just yells out the device serial number. I've tried to find ways to quiet her voice level vs music and I just don't see the option anywhere. 2) For it to be a smart speaker that is compatible with smart devices it sure doesn't seem all that smart. It still needs to be manually connected to other devices that A) that are in the same network, B) have Alexa C) Have Alexa under the same account... D) Are streaming Amazon content. Feels like 2008 all over again. The Alexa app is ok but nowhere near as intuitive as it should be. 3) Echo Dot 3 is NOT a portable, speaker as it has no battery. Maybe they're saving that feature for the 4. I've never had a desktop speaker that I couldn't take with me. There are however 3rd party devices available to remedy this. Overall, like I said, decent sound device. As long as you have stable wifi and the patience to constantly adjust the volume and to the situation you should be fine with it.
title: Decent sound quality but full of issues

And now ... to the assembly. The so-called "instructions" include a one-person, 30 minutes outline. That's garbage. It took me nearly 3 hours to get this thing together and I ended up with 4 small screws left over. Why 4 screws? Because the place where they were supposed to go had NO pre-drilled holes as indicated! I don't have a drill and wasn't about to drive around Phoenix to buy one. I was about to use an ice pick to get some holes started, but decided against that plan. Fortunately, these non-existent holes didn't mess with the assembly in the end, so while they might have shored up the tower pieces a bit, they weren't necessary. There are few words in the instructions and the artwork is not totally accurate. So, just go slow and really look at things as you proceed. Whoever writes these assembly instructions must come from another galaxy, that's for sure.

Yes, you get what you paid for and I guess this is worth the money. But I'm not sure it is worth the time and aggravation. I don't like "some assembly required" items to begin with and this one just did me in. At least I have something to put my TV on, though!

This avedio "splitter" is a must-have to use an (older) TV with a (recent) soundbar. Especially when The TV has only one HDMI input and no optical SPDIF output. And the soundbar has an optical SPDIF input but no HDMI input.

Simply plug the HDMI audio and video source into the avedio HDMI input. Then, use the HDMI cable (included with avedio) between the avedio HDMI output and the TV HDMI input. Finally, use an optical cable between the avideo SPDIF output and the soundbar optical SPIF input.

If the red HDMI indicator light is ever flashing, unplug the device from power for several minutes and plug it back in.
title: Works flawlessly.
